record.claim: With the current information, renting is the safer default until the buying case clears affordability, time-horizon and liquidity gates.

record.direction: Rent now, and do not buy unless the house passes a 5-year stay test, an all-in cost test and a post-closing cash-reserve test.

evidence.inferred: Every gate starts as unknown; the default favours the reversible option.
evidence.observed: You asked to compare renting and buying. No figures, place or timeline were given.

assumptions: You are comparing homes of similar size and area, not a cheap rental against a dream house.

needs_answers: For the home you would buy: what purchase price, down payment, loan rate, and monthly tax plus insurance are you using?
For the home you would rent: what monthly rent have you found for comparable places in the same area?
What is the minimum number of years you are confident you would stay in that area?
next_72h: Pull 3 rental listings for homes you would actually live in; record rent, deposit, maintenance and lease length.

prediction.text: If you look at listings before setting the reserve rule, the first home you like will pull the budget above the 35% gate.

reality.dependencies: Buying depends on loan approval, seller terms, inspection, taxes and market availability. Renting depends on landlord terms and lease availability.
reality.resists: Buying resists through transaction costs, hidden maintenance, rate sensitivity and reduced mobility. Renting resists through less control and possible rent increases.
reality.resources: Buying needs a down payment, closing costs, an emergency reserve and tolerance for repairs. Renting needs a deposit and accepts less customisation.

record.reply:
Default decision: rent now. Buying should not proceed until it passes three gates: you expect to stay at least 5 years, the all-in monthly ownership cost is affordable after taxes, insurance, maintenance and fees, and you still keep 6 months of essential expenses in cash after closing.

In the next 72 hours, gather 3 real rental listings, get 1 real lender quote, and compare them on a 5-year horizon. If the buy case survives that comparison, buying becomes a live option. If it does not, renting is not hesitation; it is preserving liquidity and mobility.

risk.failure_mode: Buying too early can trap you in high transaction costs, reduced liquidity, repair exposure and difficulty moving.

record.sensitivity: Buy overtakes rent only if horizon, cost and liquidity all move in its favour. Equity alone cannot carry it.
suggested_followups: We have enough savings to buy, and renting is fine too.
record.summary: Opened the decision. Rent is the default; buying waits on stay, cost and reserve.

record.reply:
Update: enough savings moves buying from impossible to possible, but not from possible to better. The key distinction is affordability versus resilience. If your savings cover the down payment and closing costs but leave you thin afterwards, buying is still fragile.

If buying leaves you with 6 months of essential expenses, an all-in monthly cost under about 35% of gross income, and a stay of at least 5 years, it becomes a serious option. For the next 72 hours: get one written lender estimate, gather three real rental comps, calculate cash left after closing, and compare both over 5 years. Do not make an offer yet.

risk.failure_mode: Buying too early can convert savings into illiquid equity while exposing you to transaction costs, repairs and reduced mobility.

record.sensitivity: Buy needs about 18 more points to overtake rent. A confirmed long stay and an all-in cost close to rent would do it.
suggested_followups: We'd stay at least 7 years; both our jobs are in Pune. Comparable 3BHK rent is ₹42,000 a month. The flat is ₹1.1 Cr; the bank quoted 8.5% for 20 years with 20% down. After down payment and closing we'd still have 8 months of expenses. Household gross income is ₹3.6 L a month.
record.summary: Savings make buying feasible. Rent stays the default until stay, cost and reserve are proven.
record.verdict: Rent by default; buying is now feasible, not yet better

record.reply:
Update: buying now passes all three protective gates, but passing the gates makes it safe, not cheaper. A ₹88 L loan at 8.5% over 20 years is an EMI of about ₹76,400. With maintenance, property tax and insurance (roughly ₹6,000), the all-in cost is about ₹82,400 a month: 23% of gross income, well inside the 35% gate. Eight months of reserve clears the 6-month gate, and 7 years clears the stay gate.

The economics still lean rent. Early on, about ₹62,000 a month of the EMI is interest. Add running costs and the return you give up on roughly ₹30 L of down payment, stamp duty and registration, and ownership's unrecoverable cost is around ₹85,000 a month against ₹42,000 rent. A price-to-rent ratio near 22 is on the expensive side. Buying wins only if the flat appreciates roughly 3.5 to 4.5% a year over 7 years, or if owning is worth that gap to you.

Next: decide what price growth you believe for this micro-market and why, and put a monthly value on owning. If either clears the gap, buying is a reasonable choice rather than a gamble.

risk.failure_mode: Buying on an unsourced growth assumption: if prices grow under 3% a year, ownership costs about ₹4 to 5 L a year more than renting for the whole stay.

record.sensitivity: Buy overtakes rent if expected price growth is above about 4% a year, or if you value owning at more than about ₹40k a month.
suggested_followups: Prices here grew about 6% a year over the last decade.
Owning is worth about ₹20,000 a month to us.
record.summary: Protective gates pass. Buying is safe but dearer; expected price growth decides it.
record.verdict: Buying is safe on every protective gate; renting is still about ₹43k a month cheaper
